title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Pipelines | PT Inspection US
description: On-site liquid penetrant testing for US pipeline stations: stainless and alloy piping, castings, non-magnetic welds. Mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Pipeline Stations and Non-Magnetic Components
html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, on United States pipeline facilities where magnetic particle methods cannot be used: stainless steel and nickel-alloy piping, small-bore instrument and chemical injection lines, valve and fitting castings, aluminum and bronze components, and welds on non-magnetic materials at compressor, pump, meter and regulator stations. Technicians are mobilized to your site with solvent-removable materials for field use. Send the component list, material and code, and request a PT inspection quote.

What dye penetrant testing is for on a pipeline system

Line pipe is carbon steel, so most surface cracking questions on the pipe itself are answered with magnetic particle inspection. Penetrant testing earns its place everywhere else. A modern station contains stainless tubing for sampling and injection, duplex or austenitic piping for corrosive service, valve bodies cast in alloy, and fittings of non-ferrous metal. None of these respond to a magnetic field, but all of them can crack at a weld or machined edge, and a surface-breaking crack of any size is a leak path.

Penetrant also works on carbon steel when magnetization is impractical, for example on complex geometry such as a branch fitting root, a threaded connection, or a surface of a small-bore socket weld where a yoke cannot be placed. For carbon steel line pipe, however, we normally recommend magnetic particle inspection on pipelines, and for wall thickness the right method is ultrasonic testing on pipelines. Penetrant shows only flaws that are open to the surface; it says nothing about what is under it.

The rules and codes behind the work

Pipelines and their stations in the United States fall under PHMSA 49 CFR Part 192 for gas and Part 195 for hazardous liquids. Design and repair follow ASME B31.8 or B31.4, and station piping may follow ASME B31.3 where the operator has so specified. Welding on pipeline facilities follows API 1104, and fabrication of alloy components often refers to ASME Section IX for qualification. The penetrant examination itself is written to ASME Section V, Article 6 and ASTM E165, and acceptance comes from the construction or repair code the operator names; for pressure piping that is commonly the criteria in the applicable ASME B31 code.

Our guide to Article 6 penetrant requirements explains what a procedure must contain. Technicians are qualified under the company written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform and interpret the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report.

Components we examine at stations and facilities

  • Stainless instrument and sample tubing. Welds on small tube runs feeding analyzers, gauges and chemical injection pumps.
  • Austenitic and duplex process piping. Welds on amine, glycol, produced-water and corrosion-inhibitor lines where the alloy was chosen for corrosive service.
  • Valve and fitting castings. Surface porosity, shrinkage and cracks on machined faces and weld ends of cast bodies, before installation or after a failed test.
  • Small-bore socket and branch welds. Locations prone to vibration fatigue near compressors and pumps.
  • Non-ferrous hardware. Aluminum cooler headers, bronze bearings and housings, and other items that fall outside magnetic inspection.
  • Weld overlay and cladding. Corrosion-resistant overlays on scraper trap closures, flanges and valve seats, where cracking at the interface matters.

Technique: getting a clean, repeatable indication

Penetrant inspection is only as good as the surface it starts on. The sequence is pre-cleaning, penetrant application, dwell, excess removal, developer application, inspection and post-cleaning. Pre-cleaning removes paint, scale, oil and weld spatter. On soft or stainless metals, aggressive grinding or blasting can smear the surface and close the opening of a crack, so we ask for a light finishing method and a chemical etch where the procedure requires it, and we do not start the examination until the surface is dry and free of cleaning residue.

Most field work uses solvent-removable visible dye with a solvent cleaner and non-aqueous developer, because the system is portable and needs no water supply. Fluorescent penetrant gives higher sensitivity when a dark area can be provided, and is used where the procedure calls for it. Dwell time follows the penetrant manufacturer and the code, usually five to thirty minutes depending on the material and the flaw type. The standard temperature window of the test surface is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit unless the procedure has been qualified for a different range; outdoor winter work often needs heated enclosures or warm blankets, and hot surfaces in summer sun need shade to avoid solvent flashing before the dwell is complete.

Material cleanliness matters for the alloys common in stations. Penetrant materials used on austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys must be low in halogens and sulfur, because residues can cause cracking in service. We select and document certified low-contaminant materials, record the batch numbers, and remove the residue after the examination. We also keep carbon-steel brushes and tools away from stainless surfaces to avoid iron contamination.

Reading and recording indications

A linear indication is a crack, lap or seam; a rounded one is typically porosity or a pit. An indication appears as bleed-out from the flaw into the developer. Technicians watch bleed-out during the developing time and again at final inspection, because a deep crack continues to bleed, while a surface scratch fades. Non-relevant indications from rough machined surfaces, weld ripple and thread roots are called out in the report with their location and the reason for the classification. Where the procedure permits it, we photograph the indication with a scale and mark its limits on the component.

Acceptance is not our call. The operator or its engineer applies the construction code, and we give the measurements and orientation they need to do it.

Showing that the test worked

A penetrant examination that shows nothing is only meaningful if the system could have shown a flaw. Before work starts, the materials are checked: penetrant, remover and developer must be from the same compatible family, within shelf life, and not contaminated. Where the procedure requires a system performance check, the technician compares the penetrant against a known cracked comparator block and records the result. Light levels at the inspection surface are measured with a meter, not estimated. These steps take little time next to a missed crack on a gas station tube run, and they are what a Level III looks for when reviewing a report.

Time controls matter as much as chemistry. Dwell and developing times are logged for each area, because a large component examined in sections can have some zones sitting longer than others. If the surface dries out or the temperature falls outside the window during the dwell, the area is cleaned and the test repeated rather than interpreted. The same applies when the developer layer is too thick: heavy white coating can bury a fine indication, so the technician applies a thin, even film and compares with the procedure.

Special cases at pipeline facilities

Threaded connections and tight clearances trap penetrant that is hard to remove, so we use solvent cleaning and avoid water-based systems on assemblies that cannot be dried. Flange faces and gasket seats are examined with care, since scoring from a damaged seat can look like a crack. Weld overlay, such as the corrosion-resistant layer on a trap closure, may be non-magnetic and is examined from the overlay surface with attention to the fusion line. After a hydrostatic test, residual moisture or inhibitor can block flaws, so the surface is dried and re-cleaned before penetrant is applied. Parts that were examined by penetrant and then need magnetic particle inspection must be thoroughly cleaned first, because penetrant residue can mask particle indications; where both methods are called for, the order is penetrant after magnetic particle, not before.

How PT compares with the other methods for pipeline hardware

ItemBest fitNotes
Stainless sample tubing weldPTNot magnetic; surface-breaking cracks only

Thickness of a corroded station elbowUTPT gives no wall data

What the report contains

  • Operator, facility, component identification and the weld or area examined, with a sketch or marked photograph.
  • Material and form, size and the surface condition when the examination began.
  • The procedure, revision and code edition behind it.
  • Penetrant system: manufacturer, product names and batch numbers, cleaner, developer, and the contaminant certification for stainless and nickel alloys.
  • Surface temperature, dwell time, developing time and the lighting level at inspection.
  • The examiner and level under the company written practice, plus the Level III who reviewed the file.
  • Each indication with type, location and size, followed by the criterion applied when the operator provides one, and any areas not examined.

What to send for a quote

  1. Component or weld list with material grades, sizes and wall thicknesses.
  2. Governing code, edition and acceptance criteria.
  3. Whether the parts are installed, in a shop, or on a skid, and surface temperature.
  4. Alloy content, so we can plan for halogen- and sulfur-controlled materials.
  5. Access: scaffolding, confined space, lockout and permit requirements.
  6. Site orientation and badging, and the report format you prefer.

Planning for stations and facilities

Station work is scheduled around outages, compressor overhauls and valve replacements. We ask for the outage plan so penetrant examinations happen after fit-up and before final insulation or painting. Gas stations have hazardous-area rules, so solvents and ignition sources are controlled, and flammable cleaners require permits. For cold sites in the Rockies or the northern plains, enclosures and warmed materials keep temperature inside the procedure window. On sites with limited ventilation, cleaning and developer sprays raise vapor concerns, and we follow the operator’s permit instructions.

Where we work in the United States

  • Houston: Gulf Coast compressor, terminal and metering stations with alloy tubing and castings.
  • Tulsa: mid-continent liquids pump stations and instrument runs.
  • Midland: Permian sour-service skids with stainless and duplex piping.
  • Oklahoma City: Anadarko compressor stations and dehydration units.
  • Kansas City: gas transmission meter and regulator stations.
  • Denver: Rockies gathering facilities with cold-weather planning.
  • Shreveport: Haynesville high-pressure gas stations with alloy components.
  • Pittsburgh: Appalachian midstream compression and processing sites.
  • Omaha: Midwest pump and compressor stations along transmission corridors.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not run in-line tools and does not calculate remaining life or intervals. We do not offer techniques for wall measurement or crack depth sizing on this page, and penetrant cannot detect subsurface flaws. See pipeline inspection services and weld inspection for the wider scope.

Training your own technicians

Operators who want their own penetrant capability can use PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, with the penetrant testing simulator, plus pipeline NDT training. The employer certifies under its written practice; we can help write it.

faq.q: When should a pipeline operator choose penetrant testing over magnetic particle?
faq.a: Choose penetrant for non-magnetic materials such as austenitic stainless, nickel alloys, aluminum and bronze, and for geometry where a magnetic yoke cannot be placed. On carbon steel line pipe, magnetic particle inspection is usually faster and more sensitive.

faq.q: Can PT find cracks under the surface?
faq.a: No. Penetrant testing only shows flaws that are open to the surface. For embedded flaws or wall thickness, the right method is ultrasonic testing, and we can pair the two on the same component.

faq.q: Which codes cover pipeline penetrant examination?
faq.a: PHMSA 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 set the regulatory frame, with ASME B31.8, B31.4 and B31.3 for design and ASME Section V, Article 6 and ASTM E165 for the method. Acceptance comes from the construction or repair code the operator names.

faq.q: Do you use special materials on stainless steel?
faq.a: Yes. For stainless and nickel alloys we use penetrant, cleaner and developer certified low in halogens and sulfur, record the batch numbers, and remove residues after the examination.

faq.q: How cold or hot can the test surface be?
faq.a: The standard window is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit unless the procedure is qualified for a different range. In cold weather we use heated enclosures, and in hot sun we shade the surface so the solvent does not evaporate during dwell.

faq.q: Is visible dye or fluorescent penetrant used in the field?
faq.a: Visible solvent-removable dye is the usual field choice because it is portable and needs no darkness. Fluorescent penetrant is used when the procedure demands higher sensitivity and a dark area can be provided.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects the indications?
faq.a: The operator or its engineer accepts or rejects them against the code named in the specification. We report type, location, size and orientation, and we note any non-relevant indications and why we classified them that way.

faq.q: What should I send to get a quote?
faq.a: Send the component or weld list with material grades and sizes, the code and acceptance criteria, whether parts are installed or in a shop, surface temperature, alloy content, access conditions and the site address.

faq.q: Can you inspect castings before they are installed?
faq.a: Yes. We examine machined faces and weld ends of cast valve bodies and fittings, either at your shop or yard or at the station before installation, and report indications against the acceptance criteria you provide.
